extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in entertainment, comedy, and celebrity controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Summarising and judging when a comedian's jokes cross lines of acceptability — e.g., sexism, ageism, disability abuse, references to tragedy, or political satire — often in the context of broadcast regulation and public reaction. The page collects instances and reactions that function as implicit criteria for what provokes complaints or regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexist/ageist content
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC Trust committee ruled that the joke about the Queen was 'sexist and ageist' (though ultimately cleared the comedian of misconduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material that denigrates individuals on the basis of sex or age can be judged unacceptable by broadcaster standards bodies; whether it constitutes 'misconduct' may depend on context and other factors. Example: impersonating the royal's voice and saying 'I’m now so old, that my p***y is haunted' was found sexist and ageist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensiveness toward disabled persons / vulnerable children
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes targeting a disabled child (Harvey Price) prompted widespread condemnation from viewers, activists and organisations including the learning disability charity Mencap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments about disabled individuals — especially minors — are likely to be judged 'disgusting' or highly offensive and can lead to upheld complaints by regulators (Ofcom in this case). Example: suggesting a child might sexually attack a parent was deemed to have 'considerable potential to be highly offensive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Derogatory comments about appearance/sexism toward women
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes about Rebecca Adlington's appearance and insinuations about her personal life were criticised as sexist and derogatory, with the BBC Trust condemning them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour that relies on demeaning a woman's looks or sexuality can be framed as sexist and attract institutional condemnation; mocking an individual's appearance (e.g., 'she looks pretty weird') is cited as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting victims vs targeting political actors (intent/context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some material (e.g., tweets about Covid death tolls) was defended as targeting the government's handling of the pandemic rather than victims themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a joke is acceptable can hinge on its intended target and perceived political satire; satirical targeting of institutions or policies may mitigate backlash compared with apparent attacks on victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to real-world tragedies and terrorism are sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke referencing the Eagles of Death Metal and the Bataclan terrorist attack was among material excised from broadcast due to sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referencing or joking about mass-casualty events or terrorism is especially likely to be censored or removed from broadcast; editorial teams may excise such jokes pre-broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes about sexual violence provoke strong controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke referencing raping and murdering TV presenter Holly Willoughby caused controversy; such references are singled out as particularly inflammatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material invoking sexual violence against named individuals triggers significant public outrage and debate; even if intended satirically, these jokes are high-risk and often judged unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and broader routine as mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Boyle argued that the context of his longer routine (which critiques 'toxic masculinity') should be taken into account and may make individuals less likely to be offended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors (audiences, press, regulators) sometimes consider whether an offensive line is part of a larger satirical critique or narrative when judging culpability; contextual framing can be used as a defense against accusations of gratuitous offensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public and organisational backlash as an evaluative signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Outrage from viewers, charities, and social media users is repeatedly cited as the consequence and evidence that a joke crossed a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters, statements from advocacy organisations (e.g., Mencap), and social-media outrage serve as practical measures of a joke's social acceptability and can precipitate investigations or regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory complaint and investigation processes (BBC Trust / Ofcom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents led to BBC Trust investigations and Ofcom complaints being upheld or examined; regulators assess material for standards like offensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcast material may be formally complained about, investigated, and adjudicated by bodies such as the BBC Trust or Ofcom; their findings (e.g., 'upheld complaints', 'considerable potential to be highly offensive') are decisive markers of unacceptable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial removal/excision pre-broadcast
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple jokes had to be excised from the final broadcast of 'Have I Got News For You' — editors removed material about the Queen and other sensitive subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasters exercise editorial control to remove contentious jokes prior to transmission; this editorial judgment functions as a practical standard of acceptability for televised comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of mistranscription and media misreporting altering perceived offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Boyle claimed that some media reports had 'mistranscribed' his joke about Holly Willoughby into 'garbled nonsense', changing how the routine was perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How jokes are reported or quoted can amplify or distort perceived offensiveness; consideration should be given to accurate transcription and the risk that partial quoting removes mitigating context.
